about.title: Commerce Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Commerce sits at a busy intersection of industrial yards, retail centers, and rail-adjacent warehouses, and that mix creates a lot of foot traffic across parking lots, loading docks, and store entrances near corridors like Telegraph Road and the I-5. A fall on wet flooring, a cracked walkway, or poorly lit stairs can happen in an instant, but proving fault under California law takes more than pointing to the hazard itself. Property owners and businesses are only responsible when they knew, or reasonably should have known, about the danger and didn't fix it or warn people in time. That's why what happens in the minutes and days after a fall matters so much: photos of the spot, witness names, and incident reports can make the difference. LawProactive doesn't practice law or handle your claim directly — we simply connect you with an independent attorney in our network who can review what happened and explain your options, free of charge and with no obligation.

whyChoose.title: Why Evidence Matters Early in a Commerce Fall Claim

items.title: Notice Has to Be Shown
items.desc: California law requires proof the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard before your fall. An attorney can help gather maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records that speak to that notice.

items.title: Surveillance Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many stores and warehouses in Commerce record over security footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation of that video can be critical to showing how the hazard formed and how long it sat there.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, a Claim
items.desc: Even if you were partly distracted or moving quickly when you fell, California's pure comparative fault rule means you may still recover a share of damages, reduced by your percentage of fault rather than blocked entirely.

items.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in Commerce?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a public entity, such as certain city-owned buildings, the deadline is much shorter and requires an early claim, so it's worth speaking with an attorney as soon as possible.

items.question: What if the fall happened at a warehouse or loading dock in Commerce?
items.answer: Commerce has a high concentration of industrial and warehouse properties near corridors like Telegraph Road and the I-5, and these sites often have different maintenance and inspection routines than retail stores. An attorney can help identify whether the property owner, a tenant, or a maintenance contractor bears responsibility.

items.question: Do I need a lawyer if the store already took a report?
items.answer: An incident report is a good start, but it's usually written from the business's perspective and may not fully capture what caused your fall. An independent attorney can review the report alongside your own account and any available video or photos to build a more complete picture.
